name: Liam Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get round on an electric bike, because our town is flat and parking is a nightmare. I work for a small agency, and I do a lot of reablement calls, which means helping people get back on their feet after a hospital stay. First call is usually Mr Bertram, a retired bus driver who had a new hip, and I help him wash and do his exercises. In between calls I'm on my phone asking an AI about whatever condition the next person has, because I'm still learning and I don't want to look clueless.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing someone go from not standing to walking to the shop in six weeks. That's a real buzz. What wears me out is the rota changing every day, and the pay, honestly. I'm still paying off the e-bike on one of those buy-now-pay-later deals, and my partner Jess is a trainee hairdresser, so neither of us earns much. We've got about two weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a bit disappointing, actually. I'd post something like, AI still helped me learn faster, so it's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's safe, because people always need help after a hospital stay. But I'm bored of being skint, and I want to move up. AI being hype doesn't get me there any faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI to learn about conditions, and I'd push the agency to let me do the fall sensors and alarm installs, because I'm good with gadgets. I'd look for a course in care technology. And I'd clear the e-bike payments by spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, but fine. Even if AI stays small, it's the reason a carer who left school at sixteen can look up Parkinson's at a bus stop and sound like he knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. What would you do with it if this is as far as it goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it to learn the stuff I'm weak on, like medicines and how to spot an infection early. I'd also use it to plan my own week better, because the rota's chaos. Dave, my boss, laughs at me for it, but he's asked me to show him twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money pressure that sits with you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The e-bike, mostly. Forty pounds a month for another eight months. If it broke or got stolen, I'd still owe the money and couldn't get to work.

say: I'd say it's a bit **disappointing**, actually.
I'd post that AI still helped me **learn faster**, so it's not nothing.
think: My job's **safe**, because people always need help after a hospital stay.
I'm **bored of being skint** and want to move up.
do: Keep using AI to **learn about conditions** between calls.
Ask to do **fall sensor** and alarm installs for the agency.
S0.quote: Even if AI stays small, it's the reason a carer who left school at sixteen can look up Parkinson's at a bus stop and sound like he knows it.
fieldNote: Liam is the agency's **gadget person**, even his boss asks him for help.
His worry is being **stuck on low pay**, not losing work.
He owes **forty pounds** a month on an e-bike he needs to get to work.

steps.text: Ask the agency to let him install fall sensors and alarms
Use an AI chatbot to study medicines between calls
Clear the e-bike loan by spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good thing, as long as the time saved goes back to clients. I'd post that care's about to get smarter and carers should get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's a chance for me. The agency's office would shrink, but someone has to run all the new tech in people's homes. If I'm the one who understands it, I get the better job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a care technology course in the first few months, the kind that teaches sensors and smart homes. I'd offer to train the other carers on the new notes app. And I'd pick up a side job setting up smart doorbells and sensors for families, maybe two evenings a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit nervous about the money while I train. AI taking the rota and the paperwork just means someone like me can finally move up from washing and lifting to running the tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your work would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The notes and the rota first, because that's office stuff. Then the medicine checks, maybe with a sensor box that tells you if someone's missed a dose. The washing and the exercises would still be me for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the agency would struggle with all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gail, who's been there fifteen years and doesn't own a smartphone. She's brilliant with clients, better than me. I'd hate to see her pushed out because of an app.

fieldNote: Liam sees Steady Disruption as a **ladder**, not a threat.

He'd build a **side income** from smart home set-ups.

steps.text: Enrol on a care technology course within three months
Train other carers on the agency's notes app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and people need to wake up. I'd be telling everyone at work to learn something new now, not in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's scary even for me. Thinking AI by 2028 means the tech side could be run by AI too, so my backup plan gets smaller. Then robots by 2031 take the hands-on bit, so I'm squeezed from both ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast, like the first month. I'd try to get a job with whoever installs the care robots, maybe as a trainee setting them up in homes. I'd use AI to learn everything I could, and Jess and I would cut back hard, no holidays, no new phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pumped and scared at the same time. My plan was always to run the care tech. If AI can run the tech by 2028, I need a plan that a machine can't copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028 and robots by 2031. Where do you fit in that gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the gap I'd be the human face of the robots, I hope. Families won't trust a robot in Nan's bedroom unless a person they know sets it up. That might be three good years, maybe more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jess actually change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop going out, cancel the streaming stuff, and Jess might move to a cheaper salon chair rent. We'd put off getting a dog, which sounds daft, but we've been talking about it for a year.

say: I'd say this is **huge** and people need to wake up.
I'd tell everyone at work to **learn something new** now.
think: Thinking AI by **2028** could run the tech side too.
I'm **squeezed** from both ends, with robots by 2031.
do: Apply to **care robot installers** as a trainee in the first month.
Use AI to **learn** everything about the robots.
Cut back hard with Jess: **no holidays**, no new phones.
S2.quote: My plan was always to run the care tech. If AI can run the tech by 2028, I need a plan that a machine can't copy.
fieldNote: Fast AGI threatens Liam's **backup plan**, not just his current job.
He bets on being the **human face** of robots for families.
He still feels in **control**, which keeps him short of alarmed.

steps.text: Apply to care robot installers as a trainee in month one
Study care robots with an AI tutor every evening
Cancel streaming and holidays with Jess
Put off getting a dog with Jess

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a proper runway, so carers should use it. I'd post about free courses whenever I found them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one suits me. I've got time to do the care tech course, get a few years installing kit, and be one of the experienced ones when the robots arrive in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the care tech course in the first year, then move to an installer by year two. I'd keep doing evening set-ups for families. I'd save, maybe a hundred a month once the e-bike's paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, but I'm not daft about it. With five years, I could be the one who knows the care robots inside out by the time they reach my town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years before thinking AI, eight before robots. Better or worse for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be in care for maybe two years, then move into the tech side. By 2034 I'd hope to be training others. But AI might take that too, so I'd have to keep moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd tell your younger self about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay in school, mate. I'd tell him that learning stuff is the one thing nobody can take off you. I'd have been miles ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for every carer to retrain if they want to. I'd tell the agency to start now, not in year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of this. I'm the kind of person who moves early, and ten years is a long time to get good at something. I'd be forty when robots come, with years of experience in the tech side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the care tech course, then maybe a proper qualification in engineering or robotics at night school. I'd build my side business with smart home set-ups. And Jess and I would save for a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. Like I can see a path. Ten years is enough time for a lad on an e-bike to become the man who fixes the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. Would you plan differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. With ten years I'd take a proper qualification instead of a quick course. I'd also give myself a couple of years to save before I jumped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your job to be in 2040?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running my own small business, setting up and fixing care robots for families in town. Maybe with one or two people working for me. And still popping in on old clients, because I'd miss them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my backup plan would get eaten before I could even start it. What would help is free courses for carers, with a bit of pay while you study, and agencies that let carers move into the tech side. I'm not scared of robots. I'm scared of being skint while I learn how to work with robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the clients who'd love it. Mr Bertram already asks me if there's an app for his exercises. Not everybody old is scared of tech.

He stays **uneasy** in slow pictures and anxious when fast AGI threatens his backup plan.
His only real fear is being **skint** while he retrains.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his care tech backup plan would vanish before he started.
